chapters.n: Ezra picks up exactly where 2 Chronicles ends. In Cyrus’s first year ruling Babylon (538 BC), God moved the Persian king’s heart to fulfill Jeremiah’s prophecy of a return after seventy years. God can work through foreign rulers to keep His promises.

f.w: the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah

f.g: Roused or awakened his will.

chapters.n: Cyrus’s decree credits Israel’s God with giving him his empire and charging him to build a temple in Jerusalem. Persian kings often honored local gods to win loyalty, but scripture sees God’s hand at work.

f.g: A title often used for Israel’s God in the Persian period.

chapters.n: Anyone among God’s people may go up to Jerusalem to rebuild the house of the God of Israel. “Go up” is the language of pilgrimage and return.

f.g: Cyrus’s decree acknowledges Him as the God who dwells in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Those who stayed behind were to support the returnees with silver, gold, goods, and animals, plus freewill offerings for the temple. This recalls Israel leaving Egypt with gifts from their neighbors — a second exodus.

f.g: Lives as a foreigner.

f.w: help him with silver, and with gold

chapters.n: The family heads of Judah and Benjamin, with priests and Levites — everyone whose spirit God stirred — prepared to go. Not all exiles returned; many had settled comfortably in Babylon. Those who went had been moved by God.

f.w: them whose spirit God had raised

chapters.n: Their neighbors supported them with silver, gold, goods, livestock, and valuables, besides freewill offerings.

f.g: Helped and encouraged them.

chapters.n: Cyrus returned the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried off and placed in his gods’ temple. The sacred vessels coming home signaled true restoration.

f.w: the vessels of the house of the LORD

chapters.n: Cyrus had Mithredath the treasurer count them out to Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah. Sheshbazzar may be the official title-holder or another name linked to Zerubbabel; scholars debate this.

f.g: A Persian name meaning ‘given by Mithra.’
The first governor of the returnees; whether he is the same as Zerubbabel is debated.

chapters.n: The inventory begins: thirty gold dishes, a thousand silver dishes, and twenty-nine knives (or pans). Careful counting showed respect for holy things.

f.g: Large dishes or basins.

chapters.n: Thirty gold bowls, 410 lesser silver bowls, and a thousand other vessels.

f.g: Of lesser quality, or duplicates.

chapters.n: There were 5,400 gold and silver items in all, which Sheshbazzar brought from Babylon to Jerusalem with the exiles. (The listed items add to 2,499, so the total may include unlisted pieces.)

f.g: The itemized numbers sum to fewer; the total probably includes items not itemized.

chapters.n: This chapter lists those from the province of Judah who returned from Babylonian exile, each to his own town. A nearly identical list appears in Nehemiah 7. Such records proved each family’s place among God’s people.

f.g: Judah, now a small province of the Persian Empire.

f.w: went up out of the captivity

chapters.n: The returnees came with eleven leaders (twelve in Nehemiah’s list, perhaps symbolizing the twelve tribes). Zerubbabel, a grandson of King Jehoiachin, and Jeshua the high priest led them.

f.g: Descendant of David, governor of Judah, and an ancestor of Jesus.
The high priest, also called Joshua.
Not the later governor Nehemiah, who came about 90 years after.

chapters.n: The list begins with families grouped by ancestor. The Parosh clan was the largest family group. Many of these family names appear again when Ezra and Nehemiah came later.

f.g: Name means ‘flea’; members of this clan returned with Ezra too.

chapters.n: Descendants of Shephatiah (“the LORD judges”) numbered 372.
The family of Arah numbered 775. Nehemiah’s parallel list gives slightly different figures for some families, perhaps from different stages of counting.
The clan of Pahath-moab, meaning “governor of Moab,” included the lines of Jeshua and Joab — 2,812 people. Perhaps an ancestor once governed Moab under David.

f.g: Literally ‘governor of Moab’ — likely a title that became a family name.

chapters.n: The family of Elam numbered 1,254. This is an Israelite clan, not the foreign nation of Elam.

f.g: Here a family name, unrelated to the nation of Elam east of Babylon.

chapters.n: The descendants of Zattu numbered 945.
The family of Zaccai — a name related to Zacchaeus, meaning “pure” — numbered 760.

f.g: Means ‘pure’ or ‘innocent’; the Greek form is Zacchaeus.

chapters.n: The family of Bani (called Binnui in Nehemiah) numbered 642.

f.g: Spelled Binnui in Nehemiah 7:15.

chapters.n: Bebai’s descendants numbered 623.
The family of Azgad — “Gad is strong” or “strong is fortune” — numbered 1,222.
Adonikam’s family (“my Lord has arisen”) numbered 666. The number here is simply a family count, with no symbolic meaning.

f.g: Means ‘my Lord has risen up.’

chapters.n: The family of Bigvai, a Persian-style name, numbered 2,056 — showing how some exile families adopted Persian names.

f.g: A Persian name; one of the leaders in v.2.

chapters.n: The descendants of Adin numbered 454.

f.g: Means ‘delicate’ or ‘luxurious.’

chapters.n: The family of Ater, through Hezekiah (likely a family branch, not the king), numbered 98.

f.g: The Ater family, of the Hezekiah branch.

chapters.n: Bezai’s descendants numbered 323.
The family of Jorah (called Hariph in Nehemiah) numbered 112.

f.g: Probably the same as Hariph in Nehemiah 7:24.

chapters.n: Hashum’s descendants numbered 223.
The children of Gibbar numbered 95. Nehemiah reads “Gibeon,” which would make this the first of the place-names that follow.

f.g: Nehemiah 7:25 reads Gibeon, a town north of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: From here the list switches from family names to hometowns. People from Bethlehem — David’s town and the future birthplace of Jesus — numbered 123.
Men of Netophah, a village near Bethlehem that produced some of David’s mighty men, numbered 56.
Men of Anathoth, the priestly village of the prophet Jeremiah, numbered 128 — a hopeful echo of Jeremiah’s purchase of land there as a sign of future return.
Those from Azmaveth, a village in Benjamin, numbered 42.

f.g: Called Beth-azmaveth in Nehemiah 7:28.

chapters.n: People of Kirjath-arim (Kirjath-jearim, where the ark once rested), Chephirah, and Beeroth — towns of the old Gibeonite league — numbered 743.

f.g: Kirjath-jearim.

chapters.n: Those of Ramah and Geba, Benjamite towns north of Jerusalem, numbered 621.
Men of Michmash, where Jonathan once won a famous victory, numbered 122.

f.g: Michmash.

chapters.n: Men of Bethel and Ai — sites tied to Abraham, Jacob, and Joshua — numbered 223.
People of Nebo — a town in Judah, not the mountain where Moses died — numbered 52.

f.g: A Judean town, distinct from Mount Nebo in Moab.

chapters.n: Those from Magbish, an otherwise unknown place, numbered 156.

f.g: A place or clan mentioned only here.

chapters.n: “The other Elam” numbered 1,254 — the same count as the first Elam in verse 7, perhaps a copying duplication or simply coincidence.
The family or town of Harim numbered 320. A priestly family of the same name appears in verse 39.
People of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, towns in the coastal plain, numbered 725. Lod is the Lydda of the book of Acts.

f.g: Later called Lydda, near modern Tel Aviv.

chapters.n: The people of Jericho, the first city conquered by Joshua, numbered 345.
Senaah was the largest group at 3,630 — perhaps not a town but a social group, as the name may mean “the hated” or lowly ones.

f.g: Perhaps meaning ‘hated’; some think it refers to a poorer class rather than a place.

chapters.n: Now the priests: descendants of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua, numbered 973. Priestly families were carefully counted because only proven descendants of Aaron could serve.

f.g: One of the twenty-four priestly divisions set up by David.

chapters.n: The priestly family of Immer numbered 1,052.
The priests of Pashur’s line numbered 1,247.
Priests of Harim’s line numbered 1,017. In all, the priests made up about a tenth of the returnees — showing how central the temple was to their hopes.
Only 74 Levites returned — strikingly few. Later Ezra also struggled to find Levites willing to come, perhaps because their duties offered fewer privileges than the priests’.
The singers, descendants of Asaph, numbered 128 — keepers of the psalms and temple music David had established.
The gatekeepers from six families numbered 139. Guarding the temple’s holiness was a sacred trust.

f.g: Gatekeepers.

chapters.n: The Nethinim were temple servants who helped the Levites. Their list begins here. Many of their names are foreign, suggesting they descended from non-Israelites who joined in temple service, like the Gibeonites.

f.g: Hebrew ‘those given’ — temple servants dedicated to assist the Levites.

chapters.n: More families of temple servants: Keros, Siaha, and Padon.
The list continues with Lebanah, Hagabah, and Akkub — humble servants remembered by name.

f.g: Means ‘white’ or ‘moon.’

chapters.n: Hagab, Shalmai, and Hanan follow. Each family that served God’s house was recorded.

f.g: Means ‘gracious.’

chapters.n: Giddel, Gahar, and Reaiah — more families of temple helpers.

f.g: Means ‘the LORD has seen.’

chapters.n: Rezin, Nekoda, and Gazzam. The name Rezin was also borne by a Syrian king — another hint of foreign ancestry among the Nethinim.
Uzza, Paseah, and Besai continue the roster.

f.g: Means ‘strength.’

chapters.n: Asnah, Mehunim, and Nephusim — the last two may refer to Meunite and Naphishite peoples, again suggesting foreign origins.

f.g: Possibly descendants of the Meunites.

chapters.n: Bakbuk, Hakupha, and Harhur — servants whose names survive only in this list.

f.g: Possibly ‘flask’ or ‘bottle.’

chapters.n: Bazluth, Mehida, and Harsha. No service in God’s house was too small to be remembered.

f.g: Possibly ‘craftsman’ or ‘magician.’

chapters.n: Barkos, Sisera, and Thamah. Sisera shares a name with the Canaanite general defeated by Deborah and Barak, but this is a later family.
Neziah and Hatipha close the list of temple servants.

f.g: Possibly ‘captured’ or ‘taken.’

chapters.n: Next come “Solomon’s servants,” descendants of foreigners Solomon conscripted for labor, who later served at the temple.
Jaalah, Darkon, and Giddel also belonged to this group.
Shephatiah, Hattil, Pochereth of Zebaim, and Ami complete Solomon’s servants. “Pochereth-hazzebaim” may mean “gazelle-keeper,” perhaps an old job title.

f.g: Possibly ‘tender of the gazelles.’

chapters.n: Together, the temple servants and Solomon’s servants numbered 392 — modest people who chose to rebuild a holy house.
Some returnees came from Babylonian towns — Tel-melah, Tel-harsa, Cherub, Addan, and Immer — but couldn’t prove their Israelite ancestry. They came anyway, joining in faith.

f.g: ‘Mound of salt’ — a settlement in Babylonia. ‘Tel’ means a mound of ruins.

f.w: could not shew their father's house
f.g: Could not prove their family lineage.

chapters.n: These families — Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda — numbered 652. They were welcomed even without records.

f.g: Not the same as the later opponent Tobiah of Nehemiah.

chapters.n: Some priestly families also lacked records, including the line of a priest who married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite — David’s loyal friend — and took her family’s name.
They searched the genealogical records but couldn’t find their names, so they were excluded from the priesthood as unqualified. Priesthood depended on proven lineage under the law of Moses.

f.g: Treated as ritually ineligible.

chapters.n: The governor ruled they could not eat the most holy food until a priest arose with Urim and Thummim to reveal God’s will. Latter-day Saints recognize the Urim and Thummim as instruments of revelation used again in translating the Book of Mormon.

f.g: A Persian title for governor (probably Zerubbabel or Sheshbazzar).
Sacred instruments for receiving revelation, kept by the high priest.

chapters.n: The total congregation was 42,360. The family figures add up to about 30,000, so the total likely includes others not listed by family (perhaps women or those from other tribes).

f.w: forty and two thousand three hundred and threescore

chapters.n: Besides them were 7,337 servants and 200 singing men and women — perhaps entertainers or professional mourners, distinct from the temple singers.
They had 736 horses and 245 mules.
They also had 435 camels and 6,720 donkeys — the practical means for a long journey of about 900 miles from Babylon to Jerusalem.

f.g: Donkeys — the main pack animals.

chapters.n: When some family heads reached the site of the Lord’s house in Jerusalem, they gave freewill offerings to rebuild it on its original site.

f.w: to set it up in his place
f.g: To rebuild it on its former foundation.

chapters.n: They gave as they were able: 61,000 gold drachmas (darics), 5,000 minas of silver, and 100 priestly garments. Each gave according to his means.

f.g: Gold darics or drachmas — coins.
Hebrew maneh (mina), about 1.25 pounds (570 g) of silver.

chapters.n: The priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and others settled in their own towns — and all Israel in theirs. The exiles were home again.
In the seventh month — the season of Israel’s most sacred festivals — the returned exiles gathered in Jerusalem “as one man,” united in purpose.

f.g: Tishri (September–October), the month of the Feast of Trumpets, Day of Atonement, and Feast of Tabernacles.

chapters.n: Jeshua the priest and Zerubbabel the governor, with their fellow priests and kinsmen, rebuilt the altar first so sacrifices could resume as Moses’ law required. Worship came before walls or buildings.

f.w: as it is written in the law of Moses

chapters.n: They set the altar on its original foundation despite fear of surrounding peoples, and offered morning and evening sacrifices. They turned fear into faith by worshipping.

f.g: On its former foundations.

chapters.n: They kept the Feast of Tabernacles as written, offering the prescribed daily sacrifices — remembering God’s care during Israel’s wilderness journey, now fitting for exiles freshly returned.

f.g: In the prescribed number for each day.

chapters.n: After that they kept the regular offerings for new moons and all the Lord’s appointed festivals, plus freewill offerings. Israel’s calendar of worship came back to life.

f.g: The daily offering that was never to cease.

chapters.n: Sacrifices began on the first day of the seventh month, even though the temple foundation was not yet laid. They didn’t wait for perfect conditions to worship.
They paid stonecutters and carpenters, and traded food, drink, and oil with Sidon and Tyre for cedar logs floated to Joppa — just as Solomon had done for the first temple — with Cyrus’s permission.

f.w: the grant that they had of Cyrus

chapters.n: In the second month of their second year back (about 536 BC), Zerubbabel and Jeshua began the work, appointing Levites aged twenty and up to supervise. The second month echoes when Solomon began building.

f.w: from twenty years old and upward

chapters.n: Jeshua and his sons, Kadmiel and his sons, and the sons of Henadad worked together to oversee the workers. Unity of leaders made the work move.

f.g: Literally ‘as one.’

chapters.n: When the foundation was laid, priests in their robes with trumpets and Levites with cymbals praised the Lord as David had ordained. They celebrated the beginning, not just the end.

They sang in alternating choirs: “He is good; his mercy endures forever toward Israel.” The people shouted with a great shout because the foundation was laid. The same song was sung at Solomon’s dedication.

f.g: Responsively, one group answering another.

f.w: he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever

chapters.n: But older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen Solomon’s temple wept aloud, while others shouted for joy. The elders grieved how humble the new start looked compared to the old glory.

f.w: that had seen the first house
f.g: Solomon’s temple had been destroyed about fifty years earlier.

chapters.n: No one could tell the shouts of joy from the sounds of weeping, and the noise was heard far away. Joy and grief mingled — a fitting picture of restoration after loss.

f.g: Could not distinguish.

f.w: the noise was heard afar off

chapters.n: When the enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard the returnees were rebuilding the temple, they took notice. Every good work tends to draw opposition.

They approached Zerubbabel and offered to help, claiming to worship the same God since Assyria’s king Esarhaddon resettled them there. They were descendants of foreigners mixed with Israelites, whose worship combined the Lord with other gods.

f.g: King of Assyria about 681–669 BC, son of Sennacherib.

f.w: we seek your God, as ye do

chapters.n: Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the leaders refused: you have no part with us; we alone will build, as Cyrus commanded. They protected the purity of worship from mixed religion.

f.w: Ye have nothing to do with us

chapters.n: Rebuffed, the local people discouraged and frightened the builders. “Weakened the hands” means to demoralize.

f.g: Discouraged; sapped their resolve.
Here, the non-exiled, mixed population surrounding Judah.

chapters.n: They even bribed Persian officials to block the project from Cyrus’s reign until Darius’s reign — about sixteen years of delay.

f.g: Bribed advisers or officials.
Darius I, who reigned 522–486 BC.

chapters.n: Ezra now jumps ahead to show this opposition continued for generations: under Ahasuerus (Xerxes, 486–465 BC) they filed an accusation against Judah. This is the same king as in the book of Esther.

f.g: Xerxes I, king of Persia.

chapters.n: Later still, under Artaxerxes (465–424 BC), officials wrote another letter in Aramaic. From here to Ezra 6:18 the original text is in Aramaic, the international language of the Persian Empire.

f.g: Aramaic — the diplomatic language of the empire; Ezra 4:8–6:18 is written in Aramaic.
Artaxerxes I, who later sent Ezra and Nehemiah.

chapters.n: Rehum the commanding officer and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes. These verses (8–23) concern rebuilding the city walls, not the temple — placed here to show a pattern of opposition.

f.g: Commanding officer or governor; literally ‘master of decree.’

chapters.n: The letter came from Rehum, Shimshai, and their colleagues representing peoples resettled from many places — judges, officials, and people from Erech, Babylon, Susa, and Elam.

f.g: People from Susa (Shushan), a Persian capital.
People from Erech (Uruk) in Babylonia.

chapters.n: These were nations the great Osnappar (probably the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal) had deported to Samaria and the province “beyond the River.”

f.g: Probably Ashurbanipal, king of Assyria (about 668–627 BC).
West of the Euphrates — the Persian province called ‘Beyond the River.’
‘And so forth’ — a letter formula, like ‘etc.’

chapters.n: The copy of the letter begins with a standard greeting from the king’s servants in the province beyond the River.
The accusation: the Jews who came from you are rebuilding that rebellious, wicked city, finishing the walls and repairing the foundations.

f.w: the rebellious and the bad city

chapters.n: If the city is rebuilt, they will stop paying taxes, tolls, and duties, and the royal treasury will suffer. The enemies appealed to the king’s self-interest.

f.g: Different kinds of taxes: tribute, poll tax, and land tax or tolls.
Damage; harm.

chapters.n: “Because we eat the king’s salt, it isn’t right for us to see him dishonored” — so we’re informing the king. They posed as loyal servants.

f.w: we have maintenance from the king's palace
f.g: Literally ‘we eat the salt of the palace’ — an idiom for being bound in loyalty to the king.
Fitting; proper.

chapters.n: They urged the king to check the royal archives, where he would find that Jerusalem had a long history of rebellion — the very reason it was destroyed. Half-truths can be powerful weapons.

f.g: Rebellion against authority.

chapters.n: If the city and walls are rebuilt, you will lose control of the whole province west of the Euphrates — an exaggerated threat.

f.g: No share or possession.

chapters.n: The king replied to Rehum, Shimshai, and their colleagues in Samaria and beyond the River with greetings.

f.g: A standard letter greeting (Aramaic shelam).

chapters.n: Artaxerxes said the letter had been translated and read clearly before him.

f.g: Read clearly, or translated and read.

chapters.n: A search of the records confirmed that Jerusalem had revolted against kings in the past.
The records also showed powerful kings had once ruled from Jerusalem over the whole region and collected tribute — a reminder of David and Solomon’s empire.
So the king ordered the work stopped until he himself gave further orders — leaving the door open, which later allowed Nehemiah’s mission.

f.w: until another commandment shall be given from me

chapters.n: Be careful to carry this out — why let harm grow against the king’s interests?
As soon as the letter was read, Rehum, Shimshai, and their associates hurried to Jerusalem and forced the Jews to stop by armed force.

f.g: By force of arms.

chapters.n: Returning to the temple story (resuming from verse 5): the work on God’s house stopped until Darius’s second year (520 BC) — about sixteen years of silence. But God was about to raise up prophets.

f.w: the second year of the reign of Darius

chapters.n: After years of stalled work, God sent two prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, to stir up the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem. Prophetic voices restarted what discouragement had stopped. Their messages are preserved in the books bearing their names.

f.g: Literally grandson of Iddo; his father was Berechiah.

chapters.n: Zerubbabel and Jeshua responded and began building again (520 BC), and the prophets were right there helping. Prophets don’t just speak; they stand with the people in the work.

f.w: the prophets of God helping them

chapters.n: Tattenai, the Persian governor of the province beyond the Euphrates, and Shethar-bozenai came asking: who authorized you to build this house and finish this structure?

f.g: Tattenai — his name appears in a Babylonian document from 502 BC as governor of the region.
Probably ‘this structure’ — the temple’s woodwork or walls.

chapters.n: They also demanded the names of the men responsible for the building. (“We” here likely reflects the source document’s voice.)

f.g: Ancient versions read ‘they said’ — the officials asked.

chapters.n: But God’s eye was watching over the Jewish elders, so the officials didn’t stop the work while waiting for Darius’s reply. God’s watchful care allowed the work to continue.

f.w: the eye of their God was upon the elders

chapters.n: Here is the copy of the letter Tattenai, Shethar-bozenai, and their officials sent to King Darius. Unlike the hostile letter in chapter 4, this one is fairly neutral and fair.

f.g: Probably a Persian term for officials or investigators.

chapters.n: The letter opens with the formal greeting: “To King Darius, all peace.”
They reported that the house of “the great God” in Judea was being built with large stones and timber in the walls, and the work was moving fast and succeeding.

f.g: Literally ‘stones of rolling’ — blocks so large they had to be rolled into place.

chapters.n: We asked the elders who gave them permission to build.
We also asked their leaders’ names so we could inform you.

f.g: Inform; report officially.

chapters.n: The elders answered with a bold testimony: we are servants of the God of heaven and earth, rebuilding the house a great king of Israel (Solomon) built long ago.

f.w: We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth

chapters.n: They honestly admitted their ancestors provoked God, so He handed them to Nebuchadnezzar, who destroyed the temple and exiled them. They owned their history.

f.w: our fathers had provoked the God of heaven

f.g: Of the Chaldean dynasty ruling Babylon.

chapters.n: But in Cyrus’s first year as king of Babylon, he issued a decree to rebuild this house of God.

f.w: a decree to build this house of God

chapters.n: Cyrus also returned the gold and silver temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken, giving them to Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor.
Cyrus told him to take the vessels to Jerusalem and rebuild God’s house on its original site.

f.g: On its original site.

chapters.n: Sheshbazzar laid the foundation, and construction had continued — slowly — ever since, but wasn’t finished. (In reality, it had been halted for years.)
The officials asked the king to search the royal archives in Babylon to see whether Cyrus really issued such a decree, and to send his decision. Truth could be verified in the records.

f.g: The royal archives where official records were kept.

chapters.n: Darius ordered a search of the archives in Babylon, where treasures and records were stored.

f.g: The archive — literally ‘house of the books.’

chapters.n: The scroll was found not in Babylon but at Ecbatana (Achmetha), the old Median capital where Cyrus spent summers. God’s providence preserved the record.

f.g: Ecbatana, modern Hamadan in Iran — a summer residence of Persian kings.

chapters.n: The memo recorded Cyrus’s decree: rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem as a place for sacrifice, with strong foundations, sixty cubits high and sixty wide.

f.g: About 90 feet; these may be maximum allowed dimensions rather than exact plans.

f.w: In the first year of Cyrus

chapters.n: It was to be built with three layers of large stone and one of timber, and the royal treasury would pay the costs. Cyrus had promised state funding!

f.w: three rows of great stones, and a row of new timber
let the expenses be given out of the king's house

chapters.n: The gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar took were also to be returned, each to its proper place in God’s house.
Darius now commands Tattenai and his colleagues: keep away from there. The investigators became protectors.

f.g: Stay away; don’t interfere.

chapters.n: Leave the work on God’s house alone; let the Jewish governor and elders rebuild it on its site.

f.g: Zerubbabel.

chapters.n: Darius goes further: the builders’ costs are to be paid promptly and in full from the royal taxes of the province — collected by the very officials who questioned them. Opposition turned into provision.

f.w: of the tribute beyond the river
f.g: From the provincial tax revenue.

chapters.n: They were to receive daily whatever the priests needed for sacrifices — bulls, rams, lambs, wheat, salt, wine, and oil — without fail.

f.g: Required with offerings.

chapters.n: Darius wanted pleasing sacrifices offered to the God of heaven and prayers for the king and his sons. Persian kings valued the prayers of their subjects’ gods.

f.w: pray for the life of the king

f.g: Pleasing aromas — acceptable offerings.

chapters.n: Anyone altering this decree would be impaled on a beam from his own house, and his house made a rubbish heap. Persian decrees carried severe penalties.

f.g: Impaled — a Persian form of execution.
A ruin or refuse heap.

chapters.n: Darius invoked the God who made His name dwell in Jerusalem to destroy any king or people who tried to harm His house. Let it be done quickly.

f.w: the God that hath caused his name to dwell there

chapters.n: Tattenai and his colleagues promptly obeyed Darius’s orders.

f.g: Diligently; with all care.

chapters.n: The elders built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah. They finished by command of the God of Israel and the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and (later) Artaxerxes. God’s command came first; kings carried it out.

f.g: Mentioned in anticipation; he later supported the temple’s service.

chapters.n: The temple was completed on the third of Adar in Darius’s sixth year — early 515 BC — about seventy years after Solomon’s temple was destroyed. This second temple stood until AD 70 and was the temple Jesus knew.

f.g: The twelfth month (February–March).

chapters.n: The Israelites — priests, Levites, and returned exiles — celebrated the temple’s dedication with joy.

f.g: Aramaic ḥanukkah — dedication.

chapters.n: They offered 100 bulls, 200 rams, and 400 lambs — modest compared to Solomon’s thousands — and twelve goats as a sin offering, one for each tribe. Though few, they saw themselves as representing all Israel.

f.w: twelve he goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel

chapters.n: They organized the priests and Levites in their divisions for service, as written in the book of Moses. Order in worship was restored.

f.w: as it is written in the book of Moses

chapters.n: The returned exiles kept the Passover on the fourteenth of the first month. (Here the text switches back from Aramaic to Hebrew.) Passover marked deliverance — fitting for a people freed from a new bondage.
The priests and Levites had all purified themselves together, and the Levites slaughtered the Passover lambs for all the exiles, the priests, and themselves.

The returned Israelites ate the Passover, along with all who had separated themselves from the impurity of the nations to seek the Lord. Converts were welcomed — the door was open to anyone who truly turned to God.

f.w: such as had separated themselves unto them
f.g: Likely people who joined Israel by forsaking idolatry, as the law allowed.

chapters.n: They kept the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread joyfully, for the Lord had given them joy and turned the heart of “the king of Assyria” (the Persian king, ruling Assyria’s former lands) to help rebuild His house. God can turn the hearts of kings.

f.w: turned the heart of the king

f.g: Darius, ruler over the old Assyrian territories — a title recalling Israel’s former oppressor now turned helper.

chapters.n: About sixty years after the temple was finished (Ezra 6), Ezra himself finally enters the story. His family line is traced back through famous priests, starting with Hilkiah, the high priest who found the lost book of the law in King Josiah’s day.

f.g: Most scholars identify him as Artaxerxes I (reigned about 465–424 BC), son of Xerxes.

chapters.n: The genealogy continues backward. Zadok was the faithful high priest in the days of David and Solomon, and his descendants became the leading priestly family.
More links in Ezra’s priestly chain. The list is shortened (some generations are skipped, which was common), but its point is clear: Ezra’s right to serve as a priest is legitimate.
These names come from the priestly records kept in 1 Chronicles 6. After the exile, proving one’s lineage mattered greatly for anyone who served at the temple.
The line reaches all the way to Aaron, Moses’ brother and Israel’s first high priest. Phinehas was remembered for his zeal for the Lord, and Ezra will show a similar zeal.

Ezra is a “ready scribe” — skilled and quick in the law of Moses, an expert teacher of scripture. The king grants everything he asks, and Ezra credits this not to his own skill but to the Lord’s hand on him.

f.g: A skilled, expert scholar of the law; a scribe copied, studied, and taught the scriptures.

f.w: the hand of the LORD his God upon him
f.g: A favorite phrase of Ezra and Nehemiah for God’s guiding help (see Ezra 7:9, 28; 8:18; Nehemiah 2:8).

chapters.n: A second group of exiles returns with Ezra, including temple workers of many kinds. This is about 458 BC, some eighty years after the first return under Zerubbabel.

f.g: Gatekeepers of the temple.
Hebrew “given ones” — temple servants who helped the Levites (the “-im” is already a Hebrew plural).

chapters.n: Ezra arrives in Jerusalem in the fifth month, roughly midsummer. The dating shows careful record keeping.

f.g: Called Ab; roughly July–August.

chapters.n: The trip took about four months and covered roughly 900 miles, following the river routes. Ezra again sees God’s “good hand” in their safe arrival.

f.w: good hand of his God upon him

chapters.n: This verse is the heart of Ezra’s character: he prepared his heart first to seek the law, then to live it, and only then to teach it. Real teaching flows out of personal study and obedience.

f.g: Literally “set” or “fixed” his heart — a firm, settled decision.

f.w: to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach

chapters.n: The king’s letter that follows (verses 12–26) is written in Aramaic, the official language of the Persian Empire. Ezra copies it into his record as proof of his authority.

f.g: Ezra 7:12-26 is in Aramaic in the original, like Ezra 4:8–6:18.

chapters.n: Artaxerxes uses the grand royal title “king of kings.” He respectfully calls the Lord “the God of heaven,” the usual Persian way of referring to Israel’s God.

f.g: A standard title of Persian emperors, who ruled over many lesser kings.

f.w: perfect peace, and at such a time
f.g: A letter greeting, roughly “greetings, and now to the point.”

chapters.n: Any Israelite in the empire who wants to go may go. No one is forced — the return is a matter of free choice.
Ezra is sent as the king’s official representative to look into how Judah is keeping its law. The “law of thy God which is in thine hand” may be a scroll of the books of Moses he brought with him.

f.g: Persian kings had a council of seven top advisers (compare Esther 1:14).

chapters.n: The king and his advisers donate silver and gold to Israel’s God. Persian kings often supported local temples, hoping to gain the favor of each land’s god.
Ezra may also collect donations throughout Babylonia, alongside the freewill offerings of the Jewish people themselves.
The money is first to buy animals and offerings for the temple altar, so that worship can go on properly.

f.g: “Meat” in KJV English means food in general; here, grain (meal) offerings.
Wine poured out at the altar alongside sacrifices.

chapters.n: The king shows great trust: whatever is left over, Ezra and his fellow leaders may use as they think God would want.
Sacred vessels are entrusted to Ezra to deliver at the temple. Ezra 8 tells how carefully he weighed and guarded them.
Any further temple needs may be paid from the royal treasury — a remarkable blank check for a small, distant province.
Artaxerxes now addresses his treasurers in the province west of the Euphrates. They must supply Ezra’s requests promptly.

f.g: West of the Euphrates — the Persian province that included Judah and its neighbors.

chapters.n: The king sets generous limits. Salt, used with every sacrifice, is given without limit.

f.g: A talent was a large weight of metal, about 75 pounds (34 kg); a hundred talents of silver was a huge sum.
A bath was a liquid measure of roughly 6 gallons (22 liters).

chapters.n: The king wants to avoid offending Israel’s God. Whatever his motives, the Lord used a foreign ruler’s respect to bless His people and His house.

f.w: why should there be wrath against the realm of the king

chapters.n: Temple workers are excused from paying taxes. This freed them to serve and showed royal support for the temple.
Ezra is given authority to appoint judges and to teach God’s law to those who do not know it. God’s law becomes the legal code for the Jewish community in the province.

f.w: teach ye them that know them not

chapters.n: Breaking God’s law now also means breaking the king’s law, with real penalties. The Persian Empire allowed local peoples to live by their own laws under royal approval.

f.g: Literally “rooting out” — being cut off from the community.

chapters.n: The text switches back from Aramaic to Hebrew and to Ezra’s own voice. He praises God, who moved the king’s heart to beautify the temple.

f.w: put such a thing as this in the king's heart

chapters.n: Ezra feels strengthened because God’s hand is upon him, and he gathers leading men to travel with him. Ezra now begins to speak in the first person, as if from his own memoir.

f.g: From here through chapter 9, Ezra narrates in the first person (“I”).

chapters.n: Ezra introduces the list of family heads who traveled with him. Recording who returned honored their sacrifice and preserved each family’s place in Israel.
First come priestly families descended from Aaron’s sons Phinehas and Ithamar, then a descendant of King David. Hattush shows that David’s royal line was still alive and among the returning exiles.

f.g: A priest of this name, not the prophet Daniel of the book of Daniel.

chapters.n: Now the lay families begin. Many of these clan names also appear in the first return (Ezra 2), so relatives were joining kin who had gone ahead decades earlier.
Pahath-moab, meaning “governor of Moab,” was a large clan already represented in the first return.
Three hundred men come with this family. The counts give men only; with wives and children the total company was several thousand people.

f.g: Some ancient versions read “of the sons of Zattu, Shechaniah,” matching Ezra 2:8.

chapters.n: The family of Adin sends fifty men to join the journey.
The clan of Elam sends seventy men. Members of this family will later be among those who confess marrying outside the covenant.
Shephatiah’s family adds eighty men.

f.g: Eighty (a score = twenty).

chapters.n: The family of Joab sends 218 men. This Joab is a clan ancestor, not David’s general.
Another household joins with 160 men, showing how widely Ezra’s call was answered.

f.g: Sixty.

chapters.n: Twenty-eight men of the family of Bebai join the company.
The clan of Azgad sends 110 men.
“The last sons” likely means the remaining members of Adonikam’s family who had not gone with the first group. Now the whole family was finally home.
The list closes with Bigvai’s family. In all, about 1,500 men are counted in verses 2–14, besides the Levites added next.
At a gathering point by a canal called Ahava, Ezra reviews the company and realizes no Levites have volunteered. Without them, the temple could not be served properly.

f.w: none of the sons of Levi
f.g: Levites assisted the priests in temple work; few had returned even in the first wave (Ezra 2:40).

chapters.n: Ezra sends a delegation of respected leaders and teachers to recruit Levites.

f.g: Teachers or wise instructors.

chapters.n: The delegation goes to Iddo, the leader of a community at Casiphia, probably a settlement of Levites and temple servants in Babylonia. Ezra gives them exact words to say.

f.g: A place in Babylonia whose exact location is unknown.

chapters.n: Ezra credits God’s good hand for the result: a wise Levite named Sherebiah arrives with his family. Sherebiah will later help Ezra teach the law.
More Levites come from the line of Merari, one of Levi’s three sons.
Many temple servants also come — far more than the Levites. Each one is recorded by name, a sign of how much they were valued.
Before the dangerous journey, Ezra calls a fast to humble the people and ask God for a safe, straight road for their families and belongings.

f.g: To humble oneself through fasting.
A straight or level road — a safe journey.

chapters.n: Ezra had told the king that God protects those who seek Him, so he felt it would show a lack of faith to ask for soldiers. He chose to rely on the Lord and prove his testimony.

f.w: The hand of our God is upon all them for good that seek him

chapters.n: They fasted and prayed, and God heard them. The short phrase “he was entreated of us” is a quiet witness that prayer works.

f.g: He listened and granted our request.

chapters.n: Ezra appoints twelve leading priests, together with leading Levites, as guardians of the treasure. The number twelve echoes the twelve tribes of Israel.
Ezra carefully weighs out every offering in front of witnesses. This openness protected the guardians from suspicion and honored the gifts.

f.g: In a world before coins were common, value was measured by weight.

chapters.n: The amounts are enormous — many tons of silver and gold. This shows how generous the king and the people had been toward the temple.

f.g: Roughly 24 tons of silver, if a talent is about 75 pounds.

chapters.n: Fine gold bowls and two vessels of polished bronze, as precious as gold, complete the treasure.

f.g: Darics — Persian gold coins; a thousand darics’ worth of gold.
Probably shining bronze, highly prized.

chapters.n: Ezra teaches that the men and the treasure are both holy — set apart for the Lord. Those who handle sacred things should be sacred in their lives too.

f.w: Ye are holy unto the LORD

chapters.n: The guardians must watch the treasure constantly and account for it in Jerusalem. Faithful stewardship means being able to report exactly what was entrusted to us.

f.g: Storerooms built around the temple courts.

chapters.n: The priests and Levites accept the charge and take responsibility for the full weight.
The company leaves on the twelfth day of the first month. God protects them from enemies and robbers along the way, answering their fast.

f.w: such as lay in wait by the way
f.g: Ambushers or bandits along the road.

f.w: twelfth day of the first month

chapters.n: After arriving, they rest three days — the same pattern Nehemiah later follows.
On the fourth day the treasure is weighed again at the temple by priests and Levites. Meremoth will later help rebuild Jerusalem’s wall.
Every item is counted, weighed, and written down. Nothing was lost — a testimony to both the guardians’ honesty and God’s protection.
The returned exiles offer sacrifices for all Israel. The repeated twelves show they saw themselves as representing all twelve tribes, not just Judah.

f.w: he goats for a sin offering
f.g: Sin offerings sought forgiveness; they pointed forward to Christ’s atoning sacrifice (Hebrews 9:12-14).

chapters.n: Ezra delivers the king’s orders to the Persian officials in the province, and they support the people and the temple. The journey of faith ends in success.

f.g: Satraps — high Persian governors over large regions.
West of the Euphrates.

chapters.n: Some months after Ezra’s arrival, local leaders report a serious problem: many Israelites, even priests and Levites, have adopted the ways of surrounding peoples. The list echoes the nations Moses warned Israel about centuries before.

f.g: The concern was not ethnicity but religion — adopting the idol worship and practices of these peoples.

f.w: the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites

chapters.n: The specific sin is marrying outside the covenant, which had led Israel into idolatry before. Worse, the leaders were the first offenders.

f.g: Israel as a people set apart for God by covenant (compare Isaiah 6:13).

chapters.n: Ezra is crushed. Tearing his clothes and pulling out his hair were ancient signs of overwhelming grief and horror.

f.g: Tore my clothing — a customary act of mourning.
Stunned, appalled, in shock.

chapters.n: Those who took God’s word seriously gather around Ezra. He sits in silent mourning all afternoon until the evening sacrifice, around 3 p.m.

f.w: trembled at the words of the God of Israel

f.g: The daily afternoon offering at the temple (Exodus 29:38-41).

chapters.n: At the hour of prayer, Ezra kneels and spreads out his hands toward heaven — a posture of pleading. His prayer follows.
Ezra’s prayer begins with shame. Notice he says “our” iniquities — though he was not guilty himself, he stands with his people and confesses as one of them.
He reviews Israel’s history: centuries of disobedience led to conquest and exile. The scattering of Israel was the direct result of breaking covenants.

f.w: delivered into the hand of the kings of the lands

f.g: Open shame and disgrace.

chapters.n: Yet God showed grace for “a little space,” preserving a remnant. A “nail” was a tent peg — a small but firm hold in God’s holy place, a fresh start.

f.w: a nail in his holy place
f.g: A tent peg — a secure foothold; compare Isaiah 22:23.
To brighten our eyes — renew life and hope.

chapters.n: Even while under Persian rule, God moved kings to let them rebuild the temple. The “wall” here likely means God’s protection rather than literal city walls, which Nehemiah would build later.

f.g: Probably a figure for safety and protection; Jerusalem’s actual walls were rebuilt under Nehemiah.

f.w: in the sight of the kings of Persia

chapters.n: After such kindness, Ezra has no excuse to offer. The honest response to God’s mercy is confession, not self-justification.
Ezra summarizes the warnings of Moses and the prophets: the land was polluted by the corrupt practices of its earlier peoples.

The command was not to intermarry with these peoples, so Israel could stay strong and pass on the land and the covenant to its children. Marriage within the covenant protects the faith of future generations.

f.w: give not your daughters unto their sons
leave it for an inheritance to your children

chapters.n: Ezra acknowledges that God punished them less than they deserved. Recognizing God’s mercy is a key step in true repentance.

f.w: punished us less than our iniquities deserve

chapters.n: Having been rescued once, should they now repeat the same sin? Ezra fears that continued rebellion would bring complete destruction.

f.g: Become related by marriage.

chapters.n: Ezra ends not by asking for anything, but by admitting God is righteous and they are guilty. He simply places the people, with their sins, before the Lord.
Ezra’s public, heartfelt prayer moves others. Without commanding anyone, his example of sorrow draws a great crowd of families who weep with him.

f.g: Lying face down on the ground in humility.
Wept bitterly.

chapters.n: Shechaniah speaks for the people. He admits the sin openly but adds a hopeful note: it is not too late to change. Interestingly, his own father’s name appears later among the offenders (verse 26).

f.g: “Strange” means foreign — wives from peoples outside the covenant who worshipped other gods.

f.w: yet now there is hope in Israel

chapters.n: He proposes a covenant to send away the foreign wives and their children. This painful step was seen as necessary to keep the small community faithful to God; it was a response to a specific crisis, not a general rule for all times.
Shechaniah urges Ezra to lead, promising the people’s support. Leaders can act with courage when they know the people stand behind them.

f.w: be of good courage, and do it

chapters.n: Ezra has the leaders and people swear an oath to follow through. A promise made before God carried great weight.
Ezra continues to fast in private, going without food and water. His grief is real, not a public show.

f.w: he did eat no bread, nor drink water

chapters.n: A summons goes out to all the returned exiles to gather in Jerusalem.

f.g: The returned exiles and their descendants.

chapters.n: Anyone who ignored the summons would lose his property and be cut off from the community. The leaders treated the matter as urgent.

f.g: Literally “devoted” — confiscated and given to the temple.

chapters.n: In December, during the cold rainy season, the people sit in the open square by the temple. They shiver both from the rain and from the seriousness of what they face.

f.g: Kislev, roughly November–December — the rainy winter season in Judah.
The two tribes that made up most of the returned community.

chapters.n: Ezra speaks plainly: by these marriages they have added to Israel’s guilt.
Ezra’s call has three parts: confess to God, do His will, and separate from what leads away from Him. These are the steps of true repentance.

f.g: Do what He desires.

chapters.n: The whole congregation agrees loudly. Their wholehearted answer shows real change of heart.

f.w: As thou hast said, so must we do

chapters.n: Practical concerns follow: too many people, too much rain, and too many cases for one day. Repentance involves careful work, not just a moment of emotion.
They propose an orderly process: each case would be heard by local elders and judges at scheduled times, until the matter was settled.
Only a few men opposed the plan (another reading is that they were put in charge of it). Either way, the vast majority supported Ezra.

f.g: The Hebrew most likely means these men “stood against” the plan; some translations read it as “were in charge of” it.

chapters.n: Ezra and the family heads form a committee and begin the hearings ten days later.

f.w: first day of the tenth month
f.g: Tebeth, roughly December–January.

chapters.n: The investigation takes three months and concludes by the first day of the new year.

f.w: first day of the first month
f.g: Nisan, roughly March–April — exactly a year after Ezra set out from Babylon (Ezra 7:9).

chapters.n: The list of offenders begins with the priests — even the family of Jeshua the high priest. Ezra does not hide the failures of the powerful.
The guilty priests pledge with a handshake to send away their wives and bring a ram as a trespass offering, as the law of Moses required for such guilt.

f.g: Shook hands on it — made a solemn pledge.

f.w: a ram of the flock for their trespass

chapters.n: Two priests from the family of Immer are named. Immer was one of the original priestly divisions.
Five priests from the family of Harim are listed.
Six priests from the family of Pashur. In all, seventeen priests were involved.
Next come six Levites, the assistants to the priests. Ezra notes that Kelaiah also went by the name Kelita; a Kelita later helps explain the law to the people.
Even temple singers and gatekeepers are included. No group of temple workers was untouched by the problem.

f.g: Gatekeepers of the temple.

chapters.n: Now the lay families, called simply “Israel.” Parosh was the largest family in the first return, and seven of its men are named.
Six men of the family of Elam — the same clan as Shechaniah, who first proposed the covenant (verse 2).
Six men from the family of Zattu are listed.
Four men of the house of Bebai, a family that had also sent men with Ezra.
Six men of the family of Bani.
Eight men of the large clan of Pahath-moab. One bears the name Bezaleel, after the skilled craftsman who built the tabernacle.
The list of Harim’s lay family begins (a different Harim from the priestly one in verse 21).
The Harim family list ends. One man is named Benjamin, after Jacob’s youngest son.
Seven men from the family of Hashum are named.
A long list from a second family called Bani (or Bigvai in some ancient versions) begins here and runs through verse 42.

f.g: Shares the name of Moses’ father (Exodus 6:20).

chapters.n: The Bani list continues. These names are otherwise unknown, but preserving them showed that each person’s repentance mattered.
More of Bani’s family. A Meremoth and an Eliashib appear here, though they are different men from the priest Meremoth (Ezra 8:33) and the high priest Eliashib (Nehemiah 3:1).
The list goes on; the repeated names show how common certain names, like Mattaniah (“gift of the LORD”), were.

f.g: Means “gift of the LORD.”

chapters.n: Three more names from this family appear.

f.g: Means “built” — a common name among the returned exiles.

chapters.n: Three more. Nathan (“he gave”) shares the name of the prophet in David’s court.

f.g: A common name meaning “he (God) has given.”

chapters.n: The unusual name Machnadebai appears only here in the Bible.
Azareel means “God has helped” — a hopeful name in a list of people choosing to repent.

f.g: Means “God has helped.”

chapters.n: The longest family list in the chapter ends with Joseph, named after the son of Jacob.
Finally, seven men from the family of Nebo. In all, about 110 men are named — a small fraction of the community, but including many leaders.
The book ends abruptly and soberly: some of these marriages had produced children, which made the separation especially painful. The issue would arise again in Nehemiah’s day.

f.w: some of them had wives by whom they had children
